title: Ad-Darr, who permits harm
hook: the one who permits harm as a test, always named beside An-Nafi' so that all is in His hand
tomorrow: Eli wants into a weekend art class. what can Amira actually give?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Mani', and two readings of a closed door: protection, or a mirror. The line: harm withheld. Some days, though, the harm isn't held back. It arrives.

The first sip of black coffee, before anyone gets used to it, is simply bitter. People who love it say the bitterness is part of the point. Yesterday's question: Dadi's knee aches in the damp. What does she say to the ache? In Amira's house, it's short. Dadi winces, rubs the knee, and says: from Him, the ache, and from Him, the sabr, the patience. Today's Name is one that needs care.
screen: `THE FIRST BITTER SIP.` → `FROM HIM, THE ACHE.` → `FROM HIM, THE PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Ad-Darr: the one who permits harm, as a test. Scholars who wrote on the Names, al-Ghazali among them, say it should never be said alone. It's named beside An-Nafi', the Benefactor, tomorrow's Name, so the two are heard together: harm and benefit, both in one hand. The Qur'an says it plainly. If Allah touches you with harm, none can lift it but Him; and if He wants good for you, none can turn His bounty back. That isn't a God who enjoys pain. It's a claim that nothing sits outside His hand, not even the ache, so the ache is neither random nor the last word. Then the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave the turn. He said the affair of a believer is a wonder: if good comes, he is grateful, and that is good for him; if harm comes, he is patient, and that is good for him too. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in that hadith, even the bad day has a door into good, and the door is patience. Patience isn't pretending. Dadi still winces. If you're carrying real pain right now, none of this says you deserved it.
screen: `NEVER SAID ALONE.` · `HARM AND BENEFIT IN ONE HAND.` · `NOT RANDOM, NOT THE LAST WORD.` · `GRATEFUL IN GOOD, PATIENT IN HARM.` · then, large: `ALL IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: If there's coffee, tea or a square of dark chocolate nearby, take one small bitter taste and let it sit on your tongue without reaching for water. Notice how the bitterness changes as you breathe. With nothing to taste, sit with one small discomfort instead, a stiff shoulder or a cold room, and let it be there, patiently, until the bell.
screen: `ONE BITTER TASTE.` · `NO WATER YET.` · `LET IT CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Ad-Darr. The one who permits harm as a test, never named alone, always beside An-Nafi', the Benefactor.
Something to hold: all is in his hand, the bitter and the sweet, and the patience too. Day fifteen sixty-five.

howItsDone: When hardship comes, Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we belong to God and to Him we return, and ask for sabr, patience.

fork.setup: you break your wrist right before the tryouts you trained for all year. a friend texts: 'everything happens for a reason, so be happy!' what's closer to today's lesson?
options: it hurts, it's in God's hand, and patience can turn it toward good.
be happy about it; pain is secretly good, so don't feel bad at all.
it's random bad luck; God isn't part of the hard parts of life.
fork.reveal: the hadith doesn't ask for happiness about harm. it says patience in harm becomes good. the wince and the patience can sit together.

original.note: Arabic: the one who permits harm, from the traditional list of the Names; said together with An-Nafi'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a God who hurts people.
what it means: nothing, not even the ache, falls outside His hand; harm is permitted as a test, beside benefit.
what a scholar hears: al-Ghazali pairs Ad-Darr with An-Nafi'; 10:107 on harm none can lift but Him; Sahih Muslim 2999 on the believer's affair.

chat.says: dadi's knee is awful in this rain. she just says 'from Him, the ache and the sabr.' how??
options: Not calling pain good. Just: it's in God's hand, and so is getting through.
She means God sent the ache to punish her for something she once did.
She means it doesn't really hurt if your faith is strong enough.
chat.meaning: Ad-Darr is named beside An-Nafi': harm and benefit in one hand. The hadith says patience in harm becomes good.
